'In 911, Tahert, which had been briefly captured by Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i in 909, had to be retaken by the Fatimid general Masala ibn Habus' (of the Miknasa); the page does not say who held it in between, so the counterpart is the page's silence. Alexandria and the Fayyum were not kept; the page dates no withdrawal. The previous holder of Barqa is not named; Egypt was an Abbasid province.
917: Palermo surrenders. 'Fatimid authority was only established more securely with the defeat of rebels and the surrender of Palermo in 917.'
917: Fez accepts Fatimid suzerainty. 'In 917 the Miknasa and its leader Masala ibn Habus, acting on behalf of their Fatimid allies, attacked Fes' and forced Yahya IV to accept it.
921: the Idrisid Yahya IV of Fez is deposed ('before deposing him in 919'; 921 is the alternative date) and Musa ibn Abul 'Afiya takes charge for the Fatimids.

union.text: the Idrisid country, left to Musa ibn Abul 'Afiya under Fatimid suzerainty

region.text: Fez, Sijilmasa and the Idrisid country round Fes

ledger.note: 921: Fez and Sijilmasa are captured. 'The first Fatimid expeditions to what is now northern Morocco occurred in 917 and 921'; 'Fez and Sijilmasa were also captured in 921.' The 921 expedition was led by Masala ibn Habus, governor of Tahert (Fatimid page); the owner of Sijilmasa is not named on the pages opened. Repair fx-01 (conflict with idrisids, 922, 501 cells): the Idrisid Dynasty page has Yahya IV forced 'to recognize Fatimid suzerainty, before deposing him in 919 or 921' and his cousin Musa ibn Abul 'Afiya, 'who had already been given charge over the rest of the country'; the idrisids dossier already records the loss of its whole 911 shape in 921 (/7), but the compiler skipped that as the mirror of this gain, which took only the two 120 km discs, so the rest of the Idrisid country stayed Idrisid until the 925 gain. The region now includes the Idrisid 911 shape.
921: the capital moves from Raqqada to the new coastal city of Mahdia. 'In 921, the city of al-Mahdiyya was established on the coast of modern-day Tunisia as the capital.'
925: the Idrisid Hasan al-Hajam seizes Fez. 'The Idrisid Hassan I al-Hajam ... managed to wrest control of Fez from 925.'
927: Musa retakes Fez for the Fatimids. 'In 927, Musa returned, captured and killed Hassan', the last time the Idrisids held power in Fez.

931: Musa ibn Abul 'Afiya takes the west over to Cordoba. 'Musa switched allegiance to the Umayyads of Cordoba in 931 in an attempt to gain more independence' (the Fatimid page dates the defection 932: 'taking the western Maghreb with him').

933: Humayd ibn Yasal defeats Musa. 'The Fatimids sent Humayd ibn Yasal, who defeated him in 933.' [Reviewer me-08-c, 2026-10-19: confidence 2: the Idrisid page says Humayd defeated Musa in 933, 'forcing him to fall back into line', and names no territory; Morocco as direct land is a reading.]

region.text: the Rif and Jbala country, the base of the Gannunid Idrisids

ledger.note: 938: the Rif becomes a Fatimid client under the Gannunid Idrisids. 'Al-Qasim al-Gannun ... ruled here from 938 until 948 in the name of the Fatimids' ('here' is the Idrisid base in the Jbala country of the Rif; the summary line reads 'ruled northern Morocco for the Fatimids').

region.text: the Rif and Jbala country, the base of the Gannunid Idrisids

ledger.note: 948: the Gannunids go over to Cordoba. 'His son Ahmad (Abul-'Aysh) recognized the Umayyads, and they took most of northern Morocco after he refused to let them occupy Tangier' (948-954).
948: the capital moves to al-Mansuriya near Kairouan. 'In 948, the capital was shifted there to al-Mansuriyya, near Kairouan, also in modern-day Tunisia.'

948: Sicily becomes a Kalbid client. 'In 948, the Fatimid caliph al-Mansur appointed the Kalbid commander al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Kalbi as governor of the island'; 'From 948 onwards, the island was governed by the Kalbid dynasty, who ruled as autonomous emirs while formally acknowledging Fatimid authority.' Cliopatria's Emirate of Sicily row resumes in 960.

minus.text: Morocco
the Rif and Jbala country, already a Gannunid client

region.text: Morocco outside the Rif and Jbala country

ledger.note: 948: Cordoba takes the rest of Morocco. Under Abul-'Aysh (Ahmad), who 'recognized the Umayyads instead', 'the Umayyads occupied the rest of northern Morocco' (948-954) while he kept only the areas around al-Basra and Asilah; the Fatimid page adds 'The Umayyads gained the upper hand again in northern Morocco during the 950s'. Confidence 2: the page names northern Morocco only, so the south is my reading, drawn to match Cliopatria, whose shape drops Morocco in 947, a year before the page. Jawhar's invasion of 958 (vassal event) restores overlordship, not direct land. [Added after review me-08-c: the 933 gain of Morocco had no loss.]

region.text: the Rif and Jbala country, the base of the Gannunid Idrisids

ledger.note: 958: Jawhar restores Fatimid overlordship over the Idrisids of the Rif. 'In 958 the Fatimids sent a new general, Jawhar, to invade Morocco. The Idrisids again accepted Fatimid overlordship.' The Fatimid page: Jawhar 'took Sijilmasa in September or October 958 and then, with the help of Ziri, his forces took Fez in November 959'.

region.text: the Hejaz, Fatimid by name from 969 (a vassal tint, not direct land)

ledger.note: 969: Mecca and Medina recognise al-Mu'izz. 'The khutba was proclaimed for the first time in the Fatimid Caliph's name in 969' at Medina (some sources say 970); at Mecca Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Hasani did so 'as soon as news of the conquest of Egypt reached him'; other estimates for the Hejaz run to 974-975.

region.text: Egypt: Fustat and the Nile Valley

ledger.note: 969: Jawhar takes Fustat and Egypt. 'On 6 February 969, the army set out' from Raqqada; Jawhar took possession of Fustat on 6 July and led the Friday prayer in the Mosque of Amr on 9 July with the sermon in al-Mu'izz's name; the Ikhshidid regime had been 'paralyzed' by Kafur's death in April 968.

970: Syria falls to the Fatimids. 'The Fatimids defeated and captured al-Hasan ibn Ubayd Allah in May 970, and Damascus fell in November 970 after a long resistance.' The Fatimid page: Jawhar's force 'successful at first and many cities, including Damascus, were occupied that same year'.

971: the Qarmatians take Damascus and march on Egypt. 'On 25 August 971, the allies captured Damascus' and sacked Ramla on 5 September; the Fatimid page: Ja'far ibn Fallah 'was surrounded and defeated' in August 971 and Fatimid rule in Syria and Palestine collapsed. The 'allies' were a coalition assembled through the Abbasid caliph al-Muti': the Qarmatians, the Hamdanid Abu Taghlib of Mosul, the Buyid Izz al-Dawla, Bedouin tribes and Ikhshidid remnants.
971: the Qarmatians invade the Delta. 'Instead of advancing directly on Fustat, however, the Qarmatians turned to the eastern Delta' (September 971).
971: the first Qarmatian invasion is beaten in 'two fierce battles on 22 and 24 December 971' at Ayn Shams.

972: Ramla is retaken. 'Ramla, the capital of Palestine, was retaken by the Fatimids in May 972, but otherwise the progress in Syria had been lost.' The holder is the Qarmatians on the Hasan al-A'sam page (they sacked Ramla on 5 September 971); this page does not name it.

972: Buluggin ibn Ziri becomes viceroy of Ifriqiya. 'When the Fatimids moved their capital to Egypt in 972, Ziri's son Buluggin ibn Ziri was appointed viceroy of Ifriqiya', confirmed 'on 2 October 972 at Sardaniya'.

973: the caliphate's centre moves to Cairo. 'In 973, the center of the caliphate was moved to the newly founded Fatimid capital of Cairo.' Al-Mu'izz reached Alexandria on 30 May 973 and crossed the Nile on 10 June (Conquest of Egypt page).

region.text: the Rif and Jbala country, the base of the Gannunid Idrisids

ledger.note: 974: Cordoba retakes the Idrisid lands. 'In 973 their general, Ghalib, invaded Morocco'; al-Hasan and other Idrisids were taken as hostages to Cordoba in 974. Buluggin 'returned to defeat the Umayyads and impose Fatimid overlordship in the western Maghreb again' in 979 (a Zirid act, not written here).

974: the second Qarmatian invasion of Egypt. After rejecting al-Mu'izz's letter al-A'sam attacked at Ayn Shams on 4 April 974; 'Once again the Delta was captured by the Qarmatians' (Conquest of Egypt page).
974: the Qarmatians are beaten. 'On 27 April, Abdallah's Fatimid army defeated al-A'sam at Jubb Umayra', and he 'barely escaped capture'.

region.text: the towns the Tzimiskes page lists for his 975 campaign (Emesa, Heliopolis, Damascus, Tiberias, Nazareth, Caesarea, Sidon, Beirut, Byblos), Jerusalem and Tripoli left out

ledger.note: 975: John Tzimiskes campaigns in Syria and Palestine. The Tzimiskes page: 'A second campaign, in 975, was aimed at Syria, where his forces took Emesa, Heliopolis, Damascus, Tiberias, Nazareth, Caesarea, Sidon, Beirut, Byblos, and Tripoli, but failed to take Jerusalem.' The Fatimid page: 'In 975, the Byzantine emperor John Tzimisces retook most of Palestine and Syria, leaving only Tripoli in Fatimid control' (the pages disagree on Tripoli, which is left out of the zone). [Rewritten after review me-08-c from a loss of the whole 'Levant' (a region far larger than the sentence, including Tripoli, never regained): by 975 the Fatimids had already lost Syria to the Qarmatian coalition (971), the Qarmatians 'remained in control of Syria' and held Damascus and Ramla to 978 (Al-Hasan al-A'sam page), nothing shows a Byzantine garrison after the campaign, and Palestine (978) and Damascus (983) come back from other parties, so the campaign is a contest, not a transfer. byzantine-empire has no event for 975: eu-05 should mirror this pair with counterpart fatimid-caliphate.]

region.text: the towns the Tzimiskes page lists for his 975 campaign (Emesa, Heliopolis, Damascus, Tiberias, Nazareth, Caesarea, Sidon, Beirut, Byblos), Jerusalem and Tripoli left out

ledger.note: 976: the campaign ends with Tzimiskes' death. The page's infobox gives 'Died: 10 January 976'; it describes no withdrawal and says nothing on how long any Byzantine gain lasted (the Byzantine dossier holds none of this ground). Palestine returns to the Fatimids in 978 and Damascus in 983 (below); the page is silent on the rest of the zone, which Cliopatria's 980 shape draws as Fatimid. [Added after review me-08-c.]
978: Tripolitania goes under Zirid overlordship. 'In 978 the Fatimids also granted Buluggin overlordship of Tripolitania.'

978: the Qarmatians leave Palestine. 'In 978, after defeating the allies, the new Fatimid caliph al-Aziz offered an annual tribute of 30,000 dinars'; the Qarmatians were to 'recognize Fatimid suzerainty, leave Palestine, and return to Bahrayn' (the Fatimid page: 'by paying off the Qarmatis with an annual tribute').
978: Palestine returns to the Fatimids as the Qarmatians withdraw; the page does not say which towns.
983: Damascus is secured. 'The Turkish ghulam Bultakin finally succeeded in occupying the city for the Fatimids in 983.' The previous holder is not named by the page.

995: the Byzantines garrison Tartus. From Basil II's campaign of April 995: his men 'occupied Tartus, which they refortified and garrisoned with Armenian troops' (the page gives no year for the sentence, which follows Basil's arrival in Syria in April 995). Confidence 2: the page names neither the previous holder nor the year, and the Fatimid page never mentions Tartus, so Fatimid ownership is the byzantine-empire dossier's reading (its /ledger/80). Tartus lies outside Cliopatria's Fatimid shape (no cell of it falls in the 990, 1018 or 1028 shapes), so no keyframe draws it: the pair is bookkeeping for the Byzantine side. [Added after review me-08-c.]

1001: Tripolitania breaks away. 'After 1001 Tripolitania broke away under the leadership of Fulful ibn Sa'id ibn Khazrun'; briefly retaken after his death in 1009, 'The Zirids finally lost Tripoli to them in 1022.'

1028: Tartus returns. Mirror of byzantine-empire /ledger/98, which is also confidence 1 (Cliopatria's Byzantine shape drops the cell in 1028); the Basil II page is silent on the end of the garrison and on any Fatimid retaking, and the Fatimid page never mentions Tartus. Outside Cliopatria's Fatimid shape, so no keyframe draws it (see 995). [Added after review me-08-c.]

1044: Sicily's Fatimid tie lapses. The page dates the fragmentation: 'In 1044, under emir Al-Hasan al-Samsam, the island devolved into four qadits'; the Fatimid page says Fatimid suzerainty 'faded' and was 'already gone' by 1060. The date is the fragmentation's, not a recorded end of recognition. [Review me-08-c: the Kalbids page dates no break from Fatimid suzerainty - 'They were formally appointed by the Fatimids, but gained, progressively, de facto autonomous rule'; 'Under Hasan as-Samsam (1040-1053) the island fragmented into small fiefdoms'; 'The Kalbids died out in 1053' - so 1044 stays at confidence 1.]

1048: the Fatimid da'i Ali al-Sulayhi takes San'a. 'In 1047 ... built a fortress'; he 'was able to capture San'a in 1048' and in 1060 'began a campaign to conquer all of Yemen, capturing Aden and Zabid'; 'the Sulayhids were able to hold on in Yemen'. Cliopatria's Sulayhid row runs 1056-1065.

1048: the Zirids renounce the Fatimids. 'The Zirids renounced the Fatimids and recognized the Abbasid Caliphs in 1048-49'; 'Sometime between 1041 and 1051'; the Fatimid page: 'In the 1040s (possibly in 1041 or 1044)'. 'In retaliation against the Zirids, the Fatimids sent the Arab tribes of the Banu Hilal and the Banu Sulaym to the Maghreb.'

1073: Atsiz takes Jerusalem. Atsiz ibn Uwaq, 'a Turkmen of the Nawaki tribe', 'conquered Jerusalem in 1073 and Damascus in 1076' amid 'the advance of the Sunni-aligned Seljuk Turks'; the page names neither city's previous holder, so that it was Fatimid is my reading (Cliopatria drops Palestine in 1072). Badr al-Jamali 'entered Cairo in January 1074'.
1076: Atsiz takes Damascus (see 1073).

ledger.counterpart: local rulers of the Levantine coast (page silent)
ledger.note: 1089: Badr secures the coast. He worked to secure 'coastal cities, such as Gaza and Ascalon, and later Tyre, Sidon, and Byblos further north in 1089'. Who held them is not named.

1098: al-Afdal retakes Jerusalem. He 'took advantage of the crusader victory at Antioch to reconquer Jerusalem in August 1098'; the Kingdom of Jerusalem page: the Fatimids 'retook it in 1098 from the Artuqids'.
1099: the crusaders take Jerusalem. 'Jerusalem was captured on 15 July' (infobox: 'Capture of Jerusalem: 15 July 1099').

1099: the coastal plain becomes a war zone. The crusader victory came through 'the defeat of the Egyptian army under al-Afdal Shahanshah at the Battle of Ascalon on 12 August' (1099); Ascalon and Gaza stay Fatimid for 54 more years.

1104: Raymond of Toulouse takes Byblos (Jubayl). The Banu Ammar page: 'The family lost Jubayl to Raymond in April 1104'; the Siege of Acre (1104) page has the Genoese fleet that 'had previously supported Raymond of Toulouse in conquering Byblos'; the Embriaco family page has it given to Ugo I Embriaco by Bertrand of Toulouse 'from about 1110'. Confidence 2: the Banu Ammar page has the Banu Ammar of Tripoli, not the Fatimids, as the loser (Fatimid authority over Tripoli lapsed about 1065 on that page), and the Byblos, County of Tripoli and Raymond IV pages give no year; the Fatimid holding to 1104 is this dossier's reading of Badr's 1089 securing ('and later Tyre, Sidon, and Byblos further north in 1089'). Cliopatria's County of Tripoli row starts in 1111. [Added after review me-08-c: the 1089 gain of Byblos had no loss.]

1110: Sidon falls to Baldwin I. The siege page: siege '19 October - 5 December 1110' (infobox), 'The city fell after 47 days', and Sidon 'had been re-fortified by the Fatimids in 1098'. The Kingdom of Jerusalem page dates it a year later: 'Baldwin captured the port cities of Acre (1104), Beirut (1110), and Sidon (1111).' Acre surrendered on 25 May 1104 to Baldwin (Siege of Acre page, 'the Fatimid governor of Acre'); neither Acre nor Beirut is written (see notes). [Moved from 1111 after review me-08-c.]
1124: Tyre falls. 'The increase of naval and military support from Venice led to the capture of Tyre that year.'

1138: the Yemeni tie ends with the Sulayhid dynasty. The Sulayhid page: the regime 'was confederate with the Cairo-based Fatimid Caliphate'; Arwa 'was recognized by the Fatimids of Egypt as the suzerain over the various Yemeni kings'; 'With her death in 1138, there was no-one left of the dynasty, and the Sulayhid era came to an end.' The page puts the capital at San'a after 1063 and at Jibla 'in about 1087', and dates no end of the Fatimid recognition, so 1138 is my reading of the tie's end. [Moved from 1065 (confidence 1, the end of Cliopatria's Sulayhid row) after review me-08-c.]

1153: Ascalon falls. 'In 1153 Baldwin launched an offensive against Ascalon ... The fortress was captured and was added to the County of Jaffa.' Egypt 'was reduced to a tributary state' of Jerusalem. [Reviewer me-08-c, 2026-10-19: confidence 2: the Kingdom of Jerusalem page names Ascalon in 1153 but not Gaza.]
1153: the fighting over the coastal plain ends with the fall of Ascalon. [Reviewer me-08-c, 2026-10-19: confidence 2: the page names Ascalon, not Gaza.]

region.text: the Hejaz, Fatimid by name from 969 (a vassal tint, not direct land)

ledger.note: 1171: the Hejaz tie ends with the caliphate. The pages opened give no later date for the Fatimid khutba at Mecca and Medina ('Badr reestablished Fatimid authority in the Hejaz' in the 1070s and 1080s). [Review me-08-c: the Sharifate of Mecca page dates no end of the Fatimid sermon - 'The Egyptian suzerainty over the Muslim holy places was solidified after the Fatimid conquest of Egypt in 969', 'the Meccan emirs maintained an ambiguous position between the Fatimids and the Seljuks of Isfahan', 'After Saladin overthrew the Fatimids in 1171, the Ayyubids aspired to establishing their sovereignty over Mecca' - so 1171 stays at confidence 1.]

1171: Saladin abolishes the Fatimid caliphate. 'In 1171, Saladin abolished the dynasty's rule and founded the Ayyubid dynasty'; infobox 'Abolished by Saladin: 17 September 1171'. Saladin had been vizier since 26 March 1169; al-Adid died on 13 September and the Abbasid khutba was read in Cairo five days later (Saladin page); Nur ad-Din had written in June 1171 telling him to restore the Abbasids.

wars.name: Sicilian revolt against the Fatimids
wars.outcome: The first governor was expelled in 912; Ibn Qurhub rebelled until 916; Palermo surrendered in 917 and Fatimid authority was made secure.

wars.name: Fatimid campaigns in Morocco
wars.outcome: Fez suzerain 917, captured 921, lost 925, retaken 927, lost to Cordoba 931 and regained 933; the Gannunids held the north for the Fatimids 938-948; Cordoba took it in 948-954; Jawhar restored overlordship from 958; Ghalib retook it in 973-974.
wars.note: The Fatimid page dates Musa's defection 932 and Jawhar's capture of Sijilmasa and Fez September-November 958-959.

wars.name: Fatimid conquest of Egypt
wars.outcome: Jawhar left Raqqada on 6 February 969, took Fustat on 6 July and had the sermon read in al-Mu'izz's name on 9 July; al-Mu'izz arrived in 973.

wars.name: Fatimid-Qarmatian wars
wars.outcome: Fatimid rule in Syria collapsed in August 1971; two Qarmatian invasions of Egypt were beaten in two battles on 22 and 24 December 971 (at Ayn Shams, per the Conquest of Egypt page) and at Jubb Umayra on 27 April 974; al-A'sam died in March 977; in 978 al-Aziz paid tribute and the Qarmatians left Palestine.

wars.name: Fatimid-Byzantine struggle for Syria

zones.text: the towns the Tzimiskes page lists for his 975 campaign (Emesa, Heliopolis, Damascus, Tiberias, Nazareth, Caesarea, Sidon, Beirut, Byblos), Jerusalem and Tripoli left out

wars.outcome: 975: the Byzantines retook most of Palestine and Syria, leaving only Tripoli (Fatimid page; the Tzimiskes page lists the towns he took and dates his death 10 January 976: carried as a contest, 975-976); a ten-year truce began in 1001; Fatak occupied Aleppo in 1017 and was killed in 1022; victory at Uqhuwana in 1029; Romanos III broke a truce and invaded northern Syria in 1030; 'In 1038 Aleppo was directly annexed by the Fatimids state for the first time.'
wars.note: No border event for Aleppo: the pages date its occupation, not its loss (gap). The 975-976 zone is the Tzimiskes campaign; byzantine-empire has no matching contest (eu-05).

wars.name: Zirid break and the Hilalian invasions
wars.outcome: The Zirids renounced the Fatimid caliphs in 1048-49; the Fatimids sent the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym; the Zirids were beaten at Haydaran on 14 April 1052 and left Kairouan for Mahdia in 1057.

wars.name: Seljuk-aligned Turkmen conquest of Palestine and Damascus
wars.outcome: Atsiz ibn Uwaq took Jerusalem in 1073 and Damascus in 1076; Badr al-Jamali entered Cairo in January 1074 and rebuilt the army.

wars.name: Crusader-Fatimid wars for the coast
wars.outcome: Jerusalem retaken August 1098 and lost 15 July 1099; the Egyptian army beaten at Ascalon on 12 August 1099; Byblos lost April 1104 (Banu Ammar page), Sidon 5 December 1110 (Siege of Sidon page; the Kingdom of Jerusalem page says 1111), Tyre 1124, Ascalon 1153.

wars.name: Crusader, Zengid and Byzantine invasions of Egypt

zones.text: the Nile Delta around Bilbeis and Damietta

wars.outcome: Amalric invaded in 1163, besieged Bilbeis with Shirkuh in 1164, was beaten at al-Babein in 1166 and pillaged Bilbeis in 1168; Manuel sent 300 ships in 1169 against Damietta; Shirkuh and then Saladin became viziers in 1169.
wars.note: The Saladin page gives 1164, 1167 (Alexandria) and the end of 1169 (Damietta).

wars.name: End of the Fatimid caliphate
wars.outcome: Saladin, vizier since 26 March 1169, abolished the caliphate after al-Adid's death in September 1171 and had the Abbasid khutba read.
wars.note: Egypt stays one state until 1171; the Ayyubid row in Cliopatria starts in 1177.

certainty.note: The Maghreb frontiers (Tahert, Fez, Sijilmasa, the Atlantic edge) are approximate and swing year by year with the Idrisid, Miknasa and Cordoban clients.
Desert edges of the Nile Valley, the Hejaz and the Syrian marches are approximate; the Crusader-Fatimid coast from 1099 is a series of garrisoned cities (Ascalon, Gaza, Tyre) rather than a line.

notes: Cliopatria's Fatimid shapes are corrected on four lines. (1) Missing land: Cyrenaica from 914 (shapes 911-959), Damascus to 1075 and the coast (Gaza, Ascalon, Tyre, Sidon, Byblos) to 1111-1153 (shapes 1028-1152). (2) Status: Ifriqiya is a Zirid viceroyalty from 972 and independent from 1048 (the Zirid dossier, af-02, draws it from 972 as its own state and asks this dossier to treat it as a client); the Hejaz and the Rif (the Gannunid Idrisids) in 938-948 and 958-974 are client tints; Sicily is a Kalbid client 948-1044; these leave the direct shapes. (3) Time: shapes run a few years early or late against the dated events (Morocco 921, Egypt 969, Jerusalem 1073). (4) The 1169-1176 shape is the Hejaz alone and wrong: Egypt is the Fatimid core to 17 September 1171. The infobox area (4.1 M km2, undated) is 2.1 times the largest Cliopatria shape (1.95 M km2); not reconciled.
